ta-l1d45q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinctions 45–48 on God's will. Having treated God's knowledge and omnipotence, Lombard treats his will, and then (Dist. 48) the conformity of our will to his. On God's will he treats what it is and in how many ways it is said, then (Dist. 46) its efficacy. He shows that God's will is his essence, answering the objection that God is then all that he wills; that his supremely good will is the cause of all that happens naturally, having no cause itself and being the first and highest cause of all species and motions; and that Scripture speaks of God's will in various ways: properly as his good pleasure (beneplacitum), and figuratively as signs of will, of which there are five (precept, prohibition, counsel, permission, operation), not all of which mean God wills what they concern. Four articles are announced: whether there is will in God; whether it is only of himself or of others too; whether his will causes what happens; and the division of his will into will of sign and will of good pleasure.
claims: God's will is his essence and the first cause of all things.
God's will is said properly as good pleasure and figuratively as five signs.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e150.summary: First argument that will does not fit God. Will is an appetite, and every appetite belongs to the imperfect, as matter desires form (Physics 1).
claims: Appetite implies imperfection.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e153.summary: Second argument. The act of will is tending to its end, and the last end does not tend to an end, and God is the end of all.
claims: The last end does not tend.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e156.summary: Third argument. Will is a moved mover, moved by the willed (the Philosopher), but God moves all while remaining unmoved (Boethius), and moves as desired (Metaphysics), the desired moving desire without being moved.
claims: Will is moved by its object.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e160.summary: Fourth argument. Will is in reason (the Philosopher, Damascene), and reason names a shadowed cognition, arising in the shadow of intelligence (Isaac), which does not fit God.
claims: Will is in reason, which is shadowed.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e163.summary: Sed contra from the many authorities of Scripture and the saints adduced in the text.
claims: Authorities ascribe will to God.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e166.summary: Second sed contra. We are most conformed to God by what is highest in us, and the will seems highest, mover of the other powers (Anselm) and freest in our nature.
claims: Will is highest in us.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e169.summary: Third sed contra. All who confess God hold him most happy, and happiness is impossible without delight (Ethics 1), and delight requires will, consisting in its complacency.
claims: Divine happiness implies delight and will.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e172.summary: Thomas's determination. In every nature with cognition there is will and delight, since whatever can know can judge the fitting and the repugnant, and what is apprehended as fitting must be willed or desired. So in us, by the twofold cognition of sense and intellect, there is a twofold appetite: will, following the intellect's apprehension, and the sensitive appetite, divided into irascible and concupiscible. Since God has intellectual cognition (Dist. 35), he has will and delight, rejoicing by one simple operation (Ethics 7), since in every knowing nature perfect and natural operation is delightful.
claims: Wherever there is cognition there is will and delight, so God has will.
God rejoices by one simple operation.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e175.summary: Reply to the first argument. Though there is will in God, there is not appetite, since appetite properly is of what is not had (Augustine), and God has his whole good in himself; even in us will is not properly appetite when joined to the willed, but love, which is of what is already had (Augustine).
claims: God has will and love, not appetite.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e179.summary: This answers the second argument too: tending to the end is incidental to will as distant from the end, but having operation about the end is essential to it, and this fits God most, who loves himself and delights in himself.
claims: Will essentially rests in its end.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e182.summary: Reply to the third argument. Will is moved only by its end, and the end of the divine will is his goodness, really the same as the will, so God is not properly a moved mover, since every mover differs from what is moved. Perhaps for this reason Plato said the first mover moves itself, as it knows and loves itself (Commentator, Physics 8), which is said only metaphorically, as the end is said to move.
claims: God's will is 'moved' only by itself, metaphorically.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e185.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The grade of appetite follows the grade of cognition: as reason surpasses sense, rational will surpasses sensitive appetite, and as the divine intellect surpasses our reason, his will surpasses ours, which the argument concluded, that will does not fit God in the mode of ours. Yet as our reason is called intellect and the divine intellect reason (Divine Names 7) by their shared immateriality, will is said of both by a common name.
claims: God's will surpasses ours as his intellect surpasses our reason.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e197.summary: First argument that God's will is only of himself. Will is of the end, choice of means (Ethics 3), and nothing but himself is the end of his operation.
claims: Will is of the end only.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e200.summary: Second argument. Will is moved by the willed, and nothing but himself can move God's will.
claims: Only God moves God's will.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e203.summary: Third argument. Each wills what is good for himself, and what is good for someone makes a difference to him whether it is or not, but no creature makes a difference to God, who needs nothing.
claims: Creatures make no difference to God.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e207.summary: Fourth argument. Means are sought only for the end, so when the end is had there is no further will of means, and the end of all creatures, divine goodness, is in God eternally.
claims: The end had, means are not willed.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e210.summary: Sed contra. Love consists in an act of will, and Wis. 11 says God loves all that exist and hates nothing he made.
claims: God loves all he made.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e213.summary: Second sed contra. As God's knowledge relates to the true, his will to the good, and his knowledge is of all truths.
claims: Will parallels knowledge.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e216.summary: Thomas's determination. As God, knowing his essence, knows all that is from him as likenesses of his truth, so willing or loving his essence he wills all that is from him as having likeness to his goodness. So what he wills first is his goodness alone; other things he wills in order to his goodness, not to acquire goodness through them, as we do in doing good to others, but to bestow some of his goodness on them, so liberality is as it were proper to him (Avicenna), since by his operation he intends no advantage to himself but wills to diffuse his goodness to others, and so Augustine says he uses us for his goodness and our benefit.
claims: God wills his goodness first and other things as sharing it, not to gain from them.
Liberality is proper to God.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e219.summary: Reply to the first argument. In the object of a power there is the material and what formally completes its character, as colour is potentially visible and actually visible only by light. So what formally completes the willed is the end, from which it has the character of good, which the Philosopher means by 'will is of the end'; means relate materially to the will's object, willed by order to the end, as colour is seen by light.
claims: The end is the formal object of will; means are its material object.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e222.summary: Reply to the second argument. What is willed as end moves and perfects the will, and so only God moves the divine will, but what is ordered to the end is willed as effected and moved by the will, as in an artisan's will, the principle of operations ordered to an end.
claims: The end moves the will; means are moved by it.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e226.summary: Reply to the third argument. God's will is only of what is his good, but not as ours, which wills its good as perfecting it as end or as a means to the end; the divine will wills its good that is itself and what is from it, not what helps it, so it makes no difference to its perfection whether what it wills exists or not.
claims: God wills goods that come from him, not goods that perfect him.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e229.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. God orders creatures to the end of his goodness not to attain it through them but that creatures acquire some likeness of divine goodness by his operation, which could not be without his willing and making.
claims: Creatures are ordered to God's goodness to share its likeness.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e241.summary: First argument that causality of things should not be ascribed to God's will. His will is only of goods, and his knowledge is a sufficient cause of all goods.
claims: Knowledge suffices as cause.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e244.summary: Second argument. God causes only by operation, and being principle of operation belongs to power, so power rather than will is the cause.
claims: Power is the principle of operation.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e247.summary: Third argument. A contingent cause never produces a necessary effect, and will is contingent, open to either, so it cannot cause necessary things, like incorruptibles.
claims: Will is contingent.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e251.summary: Fourth argument. Given a sufficient cause, other causes are superfluous, so if God's will is sufficient, all natural causes, powers of the soul, and infused habits are superfluous, which is frivolous.
claims: A sufficient first cause would make secondary causes superfluous.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e254.summary: Fifth argument. Something can be demonstrated from a sufficient cause, so 'because God willed' would demonstrate everything, making all knowledge easy and the labours of saints and philosophers superfluous, which is foolish.
claims: 'God willed it' would explain everything.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e257.summary: Sed contra. The artisan's will is the principle of all artefacts (the Philosopher), and things proceed from God as artefacts from an artisan.
claims: God is like an artisan.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e260.summary: Second sed contra. Dionysius says love draws higher things to provide for the lesser, and all things came into being by divine providence, and love is an act of will.
claims: Love moves providence.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e266.summary: Thomas's determination. A determinate work comes only from a determinate agent, so what is only potential does not act, being indeterminate to many, but form, terminating matter's potency, is called principle of action. So where active power is determined to one effect, nothing beyond complete power is needed for the effect to follow, barring defect in the recipient, as in all natural agents. God's power, being infinite, is no more determined to this than that, nor can his work be determined by matter, since he produces matter and form. So beyond power something must determine the work, and knowledge does this, knowing the proper character of the thing; but since knowledge relates to opposites, of goods and evils, something more must complete the character of cause, the will, which determinately takes one of two things it knows or can do. So the complete character of causality in things not acting by natural necessity is found first in the will (the Philosopher), which fits the will as its object is the end, the cause of causes, from which the work's determination is taken (Physics 2), and so causality of things is ascribed to the divine will.
claims: Infinite power is indeterminate; knowledge specifies, and will determines, so will completes causality.
Causality of things belongs first to God's will, directed to the end.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e269.summary: Reply to the first argument. The character of causality is not completed in knowledge without will, so will rather than knowledge is called cause.
claims: Knowledge needs will to cause.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e273.summary: Reply to the second argument. Will is the principle of operation as first commanding the work; power, in voluntary agents, is principle of the work as executing, and the character of power is to be proximate, not first, principle, so God's will rather than power is called cause.
claims: Will commands; power executes.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e276.summary: Reply to the third argument. The divine will has freedom, so it is open to either, but beyond this it has immutability, adhering immovably to what it wills once that willing is posited, and necessary beings imitate this immobility though they do not equal it; so it should not be called a contingent cause, since contingency implies mutability.
claims: God's will is free and immutable; necessary beings imitate its immobility.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e279.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The divine will's causality does not exclude the proximate causes of things, not from insufficiency but from the order of his wisdom, which disposed effects to come through other causes, so that the dignity of causing is communicated to creatures.
claims: Secondary causes share the dignity of causing.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e282.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. A demonstration giving knowledge of a thing is taken from its proximate causes, so to have knowledge of things we must seek other reasons after his will, the first and common cause, especially since we do not fully know his will so as to see in it each thing's proper reason, as he does who knows all in himself.
claims: Science seeks proximate causes beyond God's will.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e295.summary: First argument that the division of will in the text is unfitting. God's knowledge is of many things as his will is, yet no signs are assigned to knowledge, though both are equally hidden.
claims: Knowledge has no signs.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e298.summary: Second argument. A sign without its signified is false, and these signs sometimes lack their signified, since God permits evils he does not will and commands goods he does not will to happen.
claims: The signs can be false.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e301.summary: Third argument. As there are good and better, there are bad and worse, venial and mortal, yet there is only one sign for avoiding both, prohibition, so there should be only one for goods, not precept and counsel.
claims: One sign for evils, so one for goods.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e305.summary: Fourth argument. The object of will is good, and evil's happening is not good (Dist. 46), so no sign of God's will should regard it, and permission is superfluous.
claims: Permission regards evil.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e308.summary: Fifth argument. As the signs regard different things, so does the will of good pleasure, so if signs are multiplied for their objects, the will of good pleasure should be too.
claims: Will of good pleasure would be multiplied.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e311.summary: Thomas's determination. Some things are said of God properly, truly in him, others metaphorically, by likeness of proportionality to some effect, as God is called fire (Deut. 4) since as fire consumes its contrary, God consumes wickedness, so his destroying wickedness is his being fire, and likewise punishment is called his anger; since the effect is a sign of the cause, the things in which the likeness of anger or the like is found are called signs, so punishment is a sign of his anger. God wills something properly, what he truly wills and is pleased with, the will of good pleasure, or metaphorically, in that he acts like one willing by commanding, counselling, and the like, so the things in which this likeness to God's will is found are metaphorically called his wills, and since they are effects they are called signs. The signs are assigned to the divine will as concerning human affairs, which he provides for specially. A sign of will can concern ordering humans to eternal salvation or the execution of that order. To attain the end providence gives what promotes the end and what frees from impediments: as natural things tend to their ends by active powers, human will is ordered to the end by counsels and precepts and drawn back by prohibitions from sins that impede it, as providence gave animals horns and claws against attackers. Execution of the order can be by tending to the end, doing good, with the sign of operation, since God works all goods in us, or by departing from the order, doing evil, which is subject to providence not as provided but as ordered, with the sign of permission. Or better: signs of will regard present things, operation for goods and permission for evils, or future things, prohibition for evils, precept for the good all are bound to, counsel for the more perfect good not all attain, summed up in the verse: 'he commands, forbids, permits, counsels, fulfils'.
claims: God wills properly by good pleasure and metaphorically by signs: precept, prohibition, counsel, permission, operation.
The signs correspond to providence over humans: present goods and evils, future goods and evils.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e317.summary: Reply to the first argument. God's knowledge is truly and perfectly of all things, but his will is not, so he is metaphorically said to will some things he does not will simply, which is why a will of sign is assigned.
claims: Signs are needed for will, not knowledge.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e320.summary: Reply to the second argument. In everything said metaphorically, an effect that is properly the sign of something in one is the sign of the same by likeness in another, as punishment is a sign of anger in man and in God of the will to punish, called anger by likeness. So something in God corresponds to these signs, called by likeness the will of the thing, as to a precept the will to command and to order rational nature to its end, so the signs are not false.
claims: The signs correspond to something real in God.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e323.summary: Reply to the third argument. As in the disposition of natures God gives different powers, one nobler, so that one thing attains its end more perfectly, so in the disposition of humans there are different things ordering to the end, one common to all, precept, and one for the perfect, counsel. But every sin departs from the order to the end, so every sin must be avoided by everyone, without difference of grade, so only one sign is given, prohibition.
claims: Precept and counsel differ by grades; all sin must be avoided by all.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e327.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. God does not properly will evils to happen but wills something joined to them (Dist. 46), from which it follows that he permits them, so permission is the effect of some will and is called will metaphorically.
claims: Permission follows God's will of something joined to evil.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e330.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. The divine will, though of many things willed, is one, since he wills all in one thing willed per se, his goodness, as he knows all by knowing his essence.
claims: God wills all in willing his goodness.

ta-l1d45q1-d1e339.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'The philosophers' vanity attributed them to other causes' refers to those who denied an agent cause and held the world made by chance and all by necessity of nature, or held that God works immediately only in one thing, the first creature. (2) 'Only God's will is the first cause of health and sickness, rewards and punishments, graces and retributions' excludes other causes not from causality but from being first cause.
claims: God's will is the first cause; other causes are not excluded.

ta-l1d45q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 45 divides Lombard's treatment of God's will (its essence, causality, and senses, its efficacy in Dist. 46–47, and our conformity to it in Dist. 48), and announces four articles: will in God, its objects, its causality, and will of sign and of good pleasure.
claims: God's will is his essence and the first cause.

ta-l1d45q1-Dd1e142.summary: Article 1 holds that God has will and delight, since will follows intellectual cognition, and he rejoices by one simple operation. He has love, not appetite, since he possesses his whole good. Will essentially rests in its end, God's will is moved only by itself, and it surpasses ours as his intellect surpasses our reason.
claims: God has will and delight, love without appetite.

ta-l1d45q1-Dd1e189.summary: Article 2 holds that God wills his goodness first and other things as sharing its likeness, not to gain anything, so liberality is proper to him. The end is the will's formal object and means its material object, the end moves the will and means are moved by it, and creatures are ordered to share his goodness, not to perfect him.
claims: God wills creatures in willing his goodness, out of liberality.

ta-l1d45q1-Dd1e233.summary: Article 3 holds that causality of things belongs first to God's will, since his infinite power is indeterminate, knowledge specifies, and will, directed to the end, determines. Will commands and power executes. God's will is free and immutable, not contingent. Secondary causes share the dignity of causing, and science seeks proximate causes beyond his will.
claims: God's will completes the causality of his power and knowledge.

ta-l1d45q1-Dd1e287.summary: Article 4 defends the division of God's will into good pleasure, said properly, and signs, said metaphorically: precept, prohibition, counsel, permission, and operation, corresponding to providence over human goods and evils, present and future. The signs answer to something real in God and are not false. Precept and counsel differ by grades, prohibition binds all, permission follows God's will of something joined to evil, and his will is one.
claims: God's will of good pleasure is proper; the five signs are metaphorical but true.

ta-l1d45q1-Dd1e334.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 45 identifies the philosophers who denied God's immediate causality and explains that God's will as first cause does not exclude secondary causes.
claims: God's will is first cause without excluding others.

ta-l1d45q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 45 treats God's will. Article 1 holds that God has will and delight, since will follows intellect, with love but not appetite. Article 2 holds that he wills his goodness first and creatures as sharing it, out of liberality. Article 3 holds that his will completes the causality of his indeterminate power and specifying knowledge, without excluding secondary causes. Article 4 distinguishes his will of good pleasure, said properly, from the five metaphorical signs of will: precept, prohibition, counsel, permission, and operation.
claims: God has will, wills creatures out of liberality, and his will is the first cause of things.
God's will of good pleasure is distinguished from five signs of will.
